etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fastenen, from Old English fæstnian, from Proto-West Germanic *fastinōn (“to secure, fasten”). Equivalent to fast +‎ -en.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To attach or connect in a secure manner.

quote.citation: May 31, 1711, Jonathan Swift, The Examiner No. 43
quote.text: The words Whig and Tory have been pressed to the service of many successions of parties, with very different ideas fastened to them.

definitions.definition: To cause to take close effect; to make to tell; to land.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: if I can fasten but one cup upon him
